subject.name_or_desc: Prince Rupert (the quesited); the querent a very great well-willer to the Parliament

context.question: If Prince Rupert should get honour by our wars, or worst the Earl of Essex? What should become of him?
context.asked_at: Not stated in the chapter; internal evidence (Edgehill fight 'above a moneth before') places it about November–December 1642.
context.setting: Asked in time of war, about a month after the fight at Edgehill (23 October 1642), in which Essex had the better and kept the ground.

attachments.key_positions: Rupert, as a noble person of eminency, signified by the tenth house and its lord, the Sun, peregrine and in his detriment in a fixed sign; Essex signified by Venus, lady of the opposite house, in reception with Saturn, she disposing of Rupert's significator; the Moon casting her sinister aspect to the cusp of the tenth; Venus also casting a dexter aspect to the cusp of the tenth
attachments.note: Positions as stated in Lilly's prose judgment.

provenance.book: William Lilly, Christian Astrology (1647), Book II
provenance.chapter: Book II, Chap. LXXXV: if Prince Rupert should get honour by our wars, or worst the Earl of Essex; what should become of him
